prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Our sorrow had neither place nor carrier-away, and dared not hover over the child whose breath opened as transom of a frail house. Nor could we put our sorrow in the dictionary, for ghastliness already shot out its own defining in rags of fired light. Pigeons would not sleek it over their dirty coats, nor fly sorrow against the aviary's sharp fence. Each day bridgeless, each night birdless, all the nocturnals needless at the expanse of our nightwatch. But wake at the moon, we could, mumbling, are wein a horror show?—inside of sleep our shock-white minds caught on reels where a child's body breaks the heart and the mother can't know if she counts as a mother. I don't know if the child heard what wept at the bedside, orderlies snapping smelling salts from chalky bullets against all the mothers falling, all the fathers under what each branch let down: there's a hidden weight to snow.

outputs.L2: Our grief had no home and no one to bear it away, and it feared to linger above the child whose breathing cracked open like the window above a fragile doorway. We couldn't file our grief away in any dictionary, because horror had already spelled itself out in tatters of burning light. No pigeons would smooth it beneath their soiled feathers, nor would they carry grief crashing into the aviary's cutting wire. Every day without a bridge across it, every night stripped of birds, all creatures of darkness rendered pointless in the vast reach of our vigil. Yet we could rouse ourselves beneath the moon, muttering, are we trapped in a house of horrors?—within sleep our terror-blanched minds snagged on looping film where a child's small form shatters the heart and the mother cannot tell whether she still qualifies as one. I cannot say whether the child took in the sound of weeping at the bedside, the attendants cracking smelling salts like powdery cartridges against every mother collapsing, every father buried beneath whatever each limb released: snow carries a concealed heaviness.
outputs.L3:
# A Weight Without a Place

The sorrow was of such magnitude that it seemed to have nowhere to rest. It was a grief too vast for any single vessel, too heavy for any single heart, and yet it could not even bring itself to settle—could not hover gently over the fragile form of the child whose life hung by the thinnest of threads. The endangered little one lay there, and the sorrow, immense as it was, remained homeless, adrift, unable to find its proper place in the world.

This was a grief that refused every attempt at definition. It could not be contained within the borders of language, could not be pressed into words that might somehow diminish it or make it bearable. No comfort could reach it. No soothing presence, however tender, could ease its raw and relentless ache. It stood beyond the reach of consolation, a thing untouchable and unnameable.

Time itself began to lose its shape. The hours of the vigil unwound in a disorienting blur, each day and each night stripped bare of meaning, emptied of connection and purpose. Morning and evening became indistinguishable, mere markers passing in a hollow procession, offering nothing but their own relentless continuation.

Sleep brought no relief—only a nightmarish, exhausted anguish that gnawed at the edges of sanity. In those wakeful, tormented hours, the narrator began to question the very nature of reality. Deeper still ran a haunting doubt: could a mother still call herself a mother when the child she loved lay broken before her? What did the word even mean now, in the face of such helplessness?

And this suffering was not hers alone. All around the bedside gathered a collective grief, shared among mothers and fathers who had come to keep their own vigils. One by one, they buckled beneath it—collapsing under an invisible yet crushing weight, a sorrow no eye could see but every parent there could feel pressing down upon them, unbearable and absolute.
outputs.L4:
# The Vigil

There is a grief that does not know where to put itself. It gathers in the corners of the room, in the space between one breath and the next, in the hands that hover but cannot heal. The parents sit. They have sat for hours, or perhaps for days—time has lost its edges here, dissolved into the beeping of machines and the soft hiss of oxygen.

Outside the window, snow is falling. It falls without meaning, without mercy, each flake indistinguishable from the last, and somewhere in that whiteness a bird lifts from a bare branch and is gone. The mother watches it go. She thinks: *there,* and does not finish the thought. There is nowhere for the thought to land.

The child lies small beneath the sheets. So small. How can a body hold so much of the world and yet be so slight? The father's mouth moves but produces nothing. Words have failed him completely—not because he cannot find them, but because there are none. What language exists for this? What syllable could carry the weight of a parent watching helplessness take the shape of their own two useless hands?

The snow keeps falling.

Grief, it turns out, has no proper container. It cannot be wept out entirely, cannot be spoken, cannot be set down. It circles like the birds beyond the glass, restless, homeless, refusing to settle. It slips into the sterile corridors, pools beneath the fluorescent lights, presses against the walls of the throat until breathing itself becomes an act of endurance.

And the mother—

The mother is coming apart in a way that has no visible symptom. She looks at her own reflection in the darkened window and does not recognize the face that answers her. *Who is she now?* A woman is defined, perhaps, by what she can protect. And here she is, unable to protect the one thing that matters most in all the turning world. The self she believed in—capable, whole, a keeper of small warm bodies—has been quietly unmade. What remains is something raw and nameless, a creature of pure attention, watching the small chest rise and fall, rise and fall, as though the watching itself might keep it going.

This is the thing no one tells you. That love, at its extremity, becomes indistinguishable from terror. That to hold a child in this hour is to hold your own dissolution. That the fear lives underneath everything afterward, folded and hidden, a weight you carry into every ordinary day—into the grocery store, the sunlit kitchen, the moments of forgetting—until some small thing, a bird, a fall of snow, calls it up again, whole and terrible and yours.

The machines beep on.
The snow does not stop.
And the parents keep their vigil, holding what cannot be held, saying what cannot be said, becoming, in their silence, something less and something more than they have ever been.
outputs.L5:
# The Pigeons of Our City

Our neighborhood would not be the same without the pigeons that gather each morning on the old church steps. They arrive at dawn, a soft chorus of coos filling the air before most people have even stirred from their beds.

Neither rain nor cold seems to discourage them. Our feathered neighbors huddle together on ledges and rooftops, patient and unbothered by the busy world rushing beneath them. Some people find them a nuisance, but I have always admired their quiet persistence.

Our children love to watch them scatter and swirl in great gray clouds, only to settle again moments later as if nothing had happened. Nor do the pigeons hold any grudge; they return faithfully, day after day, trusting that someone will toss them a handful of crumbs.

There is a lesson in these humble birds. Neither flashy nor rare, they remind us that beauty can be found in the ordinary. Our lives are richer for their presence, even if we rarely stop to notice.

So the next time you walk through our streets, pause a moment. Watch the pigeons. Neither the pigeons nor the city would feel quite complete without one another.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, surreal prose poem about parents keeping vigil over a critically ill child in a hospital, using fractured syntax and unusual imagery of birds, snow, and light.
counterfactuals.output:
# Vigil in Three Elements

The monitors sing in the dialect of small birds we cannot answer. Green lines migrate across black glass, each pulse a starling turning, the flock of her heartbeat wheeling toward some field we are not permitted to enter.

Snow began inside the room at 3 a.m.—no, that was the ceiling tiles blurring, that was salt, that was the eye's own weather. Her father presses his forehead to the window and the cold writes its slow braille into his skull. Outside, real snow. Inside, the other kind: the settling.

We keep our hands like nests. Empty ones. We have unlearned the shape of holding, relearned it against the rails of a bed built for someone smaller than grief.

Listen: a sparrow trapped in the fluorescent hum, beating soft against the light, against the light, against the—

The doctors arrive wearing weather in their voices. *Overnight. We'll know more.* Language falls in flakes, dissolves before we catch it. We are trying to read the sky of her face. We are meteorologists of a single body.

Her mother has become a lamp. Has been burning since Tuesday. Will not be told to sleep. *If I close my eyes the snow gets in,* she says, meaning the white erasure, meaning the field where the birds go down and do not rise.

And light—god, the light here refuses mercy. It shows us everything: the tube, the bruise, the small blue moon of her fingernail. But under it, sometimes, her chest lifts. A wing. Once more. A wing.

We fold ourselves into paper cranes of waiting.
We line the sill with everything we cannot say.
Morning comes the color of thawed milk, and she is still here, still here, still—

the birds settle.
The snow holds its breath.
The light, at last, forgives its own brightness and turns
gold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental piece exploring a mother's grief and dissociation at her child's sickbed, with language that breaks grammatical convention and blends the domestic with the nightmarish.
counterfactuals.output:
# Vigil in the Key of Unbecoming

---

The thermometer says numbers I stop having. Ninety-nine point. Point. The decimal a small dark seed I could plant if I had. If I had.

Her forehead: a stove I keep my hand to. Mother-hand. This is what mothers. This is the verb of me now, to forehead, to cool-cloth, to hush.

*Hush.*

The nightlight throws her animals up the wall giraffe-long and wrong. A rabbit becomes an ear becomes a scythe. Domestic shapes going feral in the dark and I let them, I let the wallpaper flowers open their mouths because someone in this room should be screaming and it cannot be me, I am the calm one, I am the ceiling she looks up at when she surfaces.

Do I. Am I here.

There is a woman in the chair by the bed. She has my rings. She wears my tiredness like a coat two sizes. She watches the small chest go up and — wait for it — down and — wait — and this waiting is a religion now, this is the only church, the up, the wait, the down, amen, again.

*Again.*

Somewhere I am folding laundry. Somewhere the impossible small socks. I hold a sock the size of nothing, the size of a plum, of a mouse, of the first thing she ever curled her hand around which was my finger which was the whole world offered up in a fist. Somewhere the socks. Somewhere the woman who is not screaming.

The IV drips its little clock. Tick of clear. Tock of clear. Time made liquid and fed to her by a machine that loves her the way I cannot right now because to love her right now with my whole is to break my whole and then who forehead-cools, who hush.

*Hush, love. Mama's.*

Mama's what. Finish it. I dare the sentence. Mama's here Mama's got you Mama's — the words come apart like wet bread, like the crackers she wouldn't. Wouldn't eat. Turned her face and I was so *angry* then, imagine, three days ago I was angry about crackers, that woman, that idiot fortunate woman with her whole ordinary problem of a child who wouldn't.

I would give. I would give. The verb has no object big enough.

The monitor and I breathe together to keep her. If I stop she stops, I have decided this, I am the one holding, I am the rope, I am both ends of the rope pulling against my own hands.

Down the hall a vending machine hums its ugly lullaby. The nightmarish thing is not the tubes. The nightmarish thing is the *normal* — the vending machine, the nurse's clogs, the muzak, the way the world just keeps on with its stupid pretzels and its fluorescent forever while inside this one room the whole of everything is deciding.

Her eyelids flutter. A hummingbird trapped under skin.

And I lean in and I am here I am here I am fully suddenly *here*, slammed back into the woman, into the rings, into the mother-mouth that says *baby* that says *I've got you* that says the oldest sentence there is, the one before language, the low animal note, the one that means:

stay.

*Stay.*

Stay in the up. Stay in the wait. Stay in the down and rise, and rise, and

rise —
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, avant-garde paragraph about sorrow that has no place to go, incorporating images of pigeons, an aviary, moonlight, and the hidden weight of snow.
counterfactuals.output: The pigeons will not carry it—this sorrow that has no address, no country willing to receive its stamp. I have tried to release it the way you'd open an aviary at dusk, all those wings unlatching into a violet nowhere, but it circles back, roosting in the rafters of the throat. Consider how moonlight lies against the caged birds without touching them, a silver that promises transit and delivers only shine. So the grief stays, feathered and murmuring, folding itself smaller against the wire. And somewhere north of speaking, snow is accumulating its secret arithmetic—each flake a nothing, a weightlessness, until the branch remembers it is breaking. This is the hidden freight of what we cannot say: it falls so softly you mistake it for mercy, and only later, in the crack and the giving-way, do you understand what has been asked of you to hold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic prose passage in the style of contemporary experimental writers about a family's overnight watch at a dying child's bedside, with themes of shock, doubt, and maternal identity.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Long Division of Night

The clock does not keep time so much as spend it, coin by coin, into the dark hollow of the room where we have gathered like debtors.

She is small under the sheet. Smaller than the word *daughter*, which I keep turning over in my mouth like a stone I cannot swallow, cannot spit. *Daughter.* As if naming could anchor. As if I had not already begun the terrible arithmetic of subtraction.

---

Her father sits in the corner made of shadow. He has folded himself into a shape I don't recognize, a man origami'd down to angles and silence. We do not speak. What is there. The machines speak for us in their green electric liturgy, reciting the psalm of her thinning pulse.

*Blip.* A question.

*Blip.* Its unanswer.

---

I put my hand on her forehead the way my mother did, the way mothers do, and I wait to feel it—the current, the knowing, the maternal telegraph that was supposed to come installed. But there is only heat. Only a child's damp hair and my own trembling ignorance. What kind of mother cannot read her own child's leaving? What kind of animal am I, that my body did not warn me, did not scream from the marrow *this one, this one is going*?

I made her. I am supposed to unmake death by making. This is the promise no one signs but everyone believes.

---

Doubt sits down at the foot of the bed and makes itself comfortable.

*Perhaps if.* It whispers the whole catalog. *Perhaps if I had noticed the fever sooner. Perhaps if I had not slept. Perhaps if I were a different woman, a better one, a truer mother, the kind who—*

The night does not argue. The night only widens.

---

Toward the hour that has no name, the one between the last hour and the first, I lean close and breathe her breath. In. Out. I am trying to memorize it, or steal it back, or simply keep her company across the border she is walking toward, one small step at a time, in the dark, without shoes, without me.

*Stay,* I do not say. *Go gently,* I do not say. I say nothing. I am unlearning language the way she is unlearning her body, the two of us dissolving in tandem, mother and child, subject and object, the sentence and its ending.

---

Dawn will come. I know this the way I know all cruel and ordinary things. The light will pour in indifferent and gold, and I will still be a mother, or I will be the ruin where a mother stood, and I do not yet know which, and the not-knowing is the last thing we have left to share, she and I, in the long division of this night that will not, will not, *will not* end—

until it does.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an intense, imagistic prose poem where grief cannot be named or contained, moving from a hospital scene to snow, and questioning whether the speaker still counts as a mother.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Body Keeps**

They gave me a bag of your things and called it belongings. As if the small sock, the hospital band cut clean from a wrist no wider than my thumb, as if these could belong to anyone now. The nurse's mouth kept moving. I watched it the way you watch weather through glass—something happening, somewhere, to someone standing outside in it.

There is a word for a wife who loses her husband. A word for the child who buries a mother. There is no word for me. The language simply stops, the way a road stops at the edge of water and pretends it was always going to.

*

I walked out into it. Snow. The first of the year, and cruel for coming so soft, laying itself down over the parking lot, over the roofs, over the whole indifferent county like it thought it was tenderness. Like it thought covering a thing was the same as healing it. Each flake a small cold sentence I could not finish. I stood there letting them land on my open hands and melt, land and melt, because at least *that* was something arriving and leaving that I could feel the shape of.

*

Tell me what I am now. My breasts still ache and fill for a mouth that will not come. My body did not get the letter. It goes on manufacturing a love with nowhere to be spent, a river dammed at the throat, a house still warming rooms that no one enters. Am I a mother? I carried. I labored. I named. And then the naming became a stone I carry in the place where you were, heavier every day, as if grief were the thing that grows now, taking your inheritance of my cells, my sleep, my sudden animal weeping in the cereal aisle.

*

The snow keeps falling because it does not know your name. Because the world is a mouth that swallows and swallows and never once says *sorry*, never once gives back. And still I stand here, palms up, catching what I cannot hold, mothering the empty air, mothering the cold, mothering the white and vanishing nothing that is all I have left to bring in from the storm and warm against my chest and rock, and rock, and rock.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
